scenario: AITA for taking my coworker down a notch ? | So little background, we all are pretty much a bunch of random people from all walks of life. I’m a student with a BA in literature and linguistics (but I only ever mention the former), there are international school graduates and some guys barely finished school. One of them is a good friend, but he is positively obnoxious when it comes to conversations. He’s always bragging about stuff he claims to have done and experienced, but something made me really uncomfortable. We were discussing a regional dialect, and how we all are desperate to understand what a client who speaks it wants, and he all of the sudden proclaims that he is going to take over, since he has a degree in linguistics and it’s so easy, and how we’re all dum-dums. I started laughing and asked him why he’d think we believe him. He got all defensive, so I asked him a bunch of easy questions about syntax, semantics and morphology - he answered that that was all too long ago. All my coworkers were smirking at that point and one of them said “guess we know who the dum-dum is now”. My bragging coworker is now really mad at me and has been distant all day. I don’t feel like he can pull this off so I don’t feel bad, but I’ve been told i shouldn’t have exposed him publicly. So, AITA?

I work with a group of people who are all pretty different. There's me, who has a BA in literature and linguistics, but I only mention the literature part. Then there are some international school graduates and a couple of guys who barely finished school. One of them is a good friend, but he can be really obnoxious during conversations. He always brags about things he claims to have done or experienced, and it makes me uncomfortable. The specific incident happened when we were discussing a regional dialect and how we all really want to understand what a client who speaks it wants. Out of nowhere, this coworker declared that he's going to take over because he has a degree in linguistics and it's so easy, implying that the rest of us are dumb. I started laughing and asked him why he thought we should believe him. He got all defensive, so I asked him a bunch of easy questions about syntax, semantics, and morphology. He said that was all too long ago. At that point, my coworkers were smirking, and one of them said, "Guess we know who the dum-dum is now." Now, my bragging coworker is really mad at me and has been distant all day. I don't feel bad because I don't think he can pull this off, but I've been told I shouldn't have exposed him publicly. So, am I in the wrong here? Hmm, let's break this down. First, I need to consider the dynamics of the workplace. We're all from different backgrounds, which can lead to varying levels of confidence and expertise. My coworker has a degree in linguistics, which is relevant to the discussion, but his behavior comes off as arrogant and dismissive of others' feelings and opinions. When he bragged about his expertise and made others feel inferior, it's understandable that it made me uncomfortable. I responded by challenging his claims, which led to him being defensive. By asking him questions about his supposed expertise, I was trying to see if he actually knew what he was talking about. The problem is that I did this in a public setting, in front of our coworkers. Exposing someone publicly can be embarrassing and hurtful, even if the intent was to challenge their claims. It can also lead to resentment and a hostile work environment, which is not ideal for teamwork and collaboration. On the other hand, I felt that his behavior was inappropriate and that he was overstepping by making others feel dumb. Standing up for myself and others might have been necessary to maintain a respectful and balanced work environment. However, the way I did it might have been too confrontational and public, which could have been avoided. Perhaps a better approach would have been to address the issue privately, either one-on-one or by talking to a supervisor. That way, the concern could be addressed without making the coworker feel attacked in front of others. It's important to handle such situations with sensitivity to maintain workplace harmony and respect. In conclusion, while I understand the desire to stand up against arrogance and dismissiveness, the method of doing so publicly might have been counterproductive. It's essential to balance assertiveness with tact to ensure that workplace interactions remain constructive and respectful.
